strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-explored problem: personalized federated learning that jointly handles both data heterogeneity (distinct tasks per client, temporal distribution shifts) and model heterogeneity (different architectures), moving beyond the synthetic non-i.i.d. splits common in prior PFL work.

DRAKE is a substantial benchmarking contribution: 40 tasks from 19 datasets with task heterogeneity, dynamic distribution shifts, and unseen-task evaluation, and the comparison table (Tab. 1) clearly positions it against existing FL benchmarks.

The proposed components are well-motivated and reasonably principled: SIMA uses decayed last-layer gradients from a small frozen model for cheap task-similarity estimation, and PQ-LoRA's dimension-invariant P/Q modules enable aggregation across heterogeneous hidden dimensions and depths, with block-wise alignment (CKA analysis in A.7) and CCA-based weight alignment.

Empirical evaluation is thorough: multiple benchmarks (DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-Aya, Fed-LLM), static/dynamic setups, homogeneous and heterogeneous configurations (2 and 3 model families), 8 strong baselines including SFT, 3 random seeds with standard deviations, per-client analyses, fast-adaptation experiments, compute/memory cost analysis, and extensive ablations (SIMA variants, weight alignment, rank r, number of blocks N_B).

The method is computationally practical (~10% FLOPs overhead over SFT, ~5% memory overhead) and theoretically supported (zero aggregation error when freezing A/B; capacity argument for orthogonal initialization), and transparency items (hyperparameters, hardware, limitations, impact statement) are well handled in the appendix.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: similarity-based weighted aggregation via gradient cosine similarity and EMA decay are relatively straightforward combinations of known ideas, and PQ-LoRA is conceptually simple (inserting small dimension-invariant modules plus alignment). The theoretical results (Theorems 1-2) are near-trivial and mainly justify design choices rather than providing new insight.

The benchmark, while large, is curated from existing public datasets with subsampling and task re-partitioning; it is a useful resource but its construction involves somewhat arbitrary design choices (e.g., task splits via keywords/GPT judgment), and its statistical grounding (e.g., how representative the shifts are of real deployments) is not deeply validated.

Scale is limited: at most 10 clients, 20 communication rounds, and models up to 8B parameters (with the vision encoder fixed to CLIP ViT-L in all variants). Real-world FL typically involves many more clients; the authors acknowledge this in A.19, but it weakens the 'real-world' positioning.

Gains over SFT are sometimes modest or client-dependent (e.g., Tab. 3: gains of ~0.1-0.3 for some clients), and the ablation of PQ-LoRA alone (Tab. 5) shows SIMA adds little beyond PQ-LoRA on DRAKE 'Self'/'Others' in some metrics, leaving the marginal contribution of each component somewhat unclear.
Code and data are not released at submission time despite the benchmark being a central contribution, which limits reproducibility and community adoption at review time.

Baselines under model heterogeneity are combined with Fed-ET, which may not be the strongest possible heterogeneous-model configuration, and evaluation for Fed-Aya relies on GPT-4-as-judge, which introduces potential evaluation noise/bias.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and underexplored problem: jointly addressing data and model heterogeneity in multi-modal personalized federated learning, and positions it well against prior federated distillation and LoRA-alignment methods (HETLoRA, FlexLoRA, FedMKT, PerAda).

PQ-LoRA is a clean technical idea: dimension-invariant modules (P, Q) whose size depends only on rank r enable weight sharing across architectures with different hidden dimensions and depths, complemented by block-wise layer alignment (justified empirically with CKA) and weight alignment via MSE/CCA with orthogonality-preserving post-processing.

The DRAKE benchmark is broad (40 tasks from 19 datasets, ~375k images), includes unseen-task evaluation for generalization/fast adaptation, and the comparison table against prior FL benchmarks is informative.

The empirical study is extensive: static and dynamic setups, multiple benchmarks (DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-Aya, Fed-LLM), homogeneous and heterogeneous settings, multiple seeds with error bars, thorough ablations (rank r, NB, alignment, decayed gradients), and a careful compute/memory cost analysis (~10% FLOPs overhead vs SFT).

Honest reporting of weak results: the paper transparently shows marginal or negative per-client gains vs SFT for some clients and attributes the modest average improvements to SFT being a strong personalization baseline.
weaknesses: The claimed 'model heterogeneity' is much weaker than advertised. All client models share the identical vision encoder (CLIP ViT-L/336px), so heterogeneity is confined to the LLM backbone within LLaVA-1.5 (and its Llama/Qwen variants). True cross-architecture heterogeneity (different vision towers, different MLLM families, different connector types) is never tested, undermining the central real-world claim.

Scale is very limited: at most 10 clients (acknowledged as a limitation), 20 communication rounds, and small models (0.5B–8B). Federated learning conclusions at this scale may not transfer to realistic settings with many clients, larger models, or partial participation.

The alignment procedure for PQ-LoRA requires public data Dp (a subset of the MLLMs' pre-training data) on the server, plus a designated 'pivot' model. This weakens the decentralized/privacy narrative that motivates the work, and the sensitivity to the choice of public data is not analyzed. Sharing aligned A/B-derived representations could also leak task information, which is not discussed.

Several gains over baselines, including SFT, are modest (often 1–3% on average, with some clients showing losses), and the 'Others' evaluation metric (token-overlap accuracy on other clients' tasks) is an unclear proxy for generalization; the practical significance of the 'Others' improvements is not convincingly established.

SIMA relies on a heuristic similarity measure (cosine of last-layer gradients from a small frozen model, EMA-decayed) whose effectiveness plausibly depends on how well that frozen model's loss surface reflects task relatedness; the theoretical justification is thin, and the ablation gains over simpler variants (frozen-model gradients) are small (~0.5–0.6%).

The DRAKE benchmark is largely a re-packaging and task-wise re-splitting of existing public datasets (Co-Instruct, SEED-Bench-2, IconQA, DEMON subsets, etc.); the 'first benchmark' claims should be tempered, and the curation choices (subsampling, keyword/GPT-based task splits) lack validation that the resulting tasks are well-formed.

Theory contributions are shallow: Theorem 2 (zero aggregation error when A and B are frozen) is nearly trivial, and Theorem 1 (span of r^2 outer products with orthogonal bases) is a straightforward linear-algebra fact. Freezing A and B also drastically reduces trainable capacity, and the finding that performance is insensitive to this is asserted rather than deeply analyzed.

Presentation issues reduce confidence: duplicated references ([125]/[126]), a citation to an 'Anonymous, Submitted to ACL, under review' work ([4]), typos and formatting artifacts in tables (e.g., '51,23', '81/98'), and no code/data release at submission time despite the benchmark being a central contribution, which limits verifiability of the main claims.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and important gap: most personalized federated learning (PFL) work evaluates in simulated settings, addressing either data or model heterogeneity in isolation. Jointly addressing both, with a concrete method (FedMosaic = SIMA + PQ-LoRA), is a meaningful contribution.

The DRAKE benchmark is a substantial community resource: 40 tasks from 19 datasets, spanning VQA, visual reasoning, and visual relation detection, with progressive distribution shifts and unseen-task evaluation. Table 1 clearly positions it against prior FL benchmarks, and the multi-modal federated continual learning scenario it enables appears genuinely novel.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four benchmarks (DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-Aya, Fed-LLM), two model families (Llama-3 and Qwen2.5 based LLaVA), static and dynamic setups, homogeneous and heterogeneous configurations, 3 random seeds with error bars, per-client analyses, and an honest discussion of where SFT remains competitive.

Thorough ablations cover each component (PQ-LoRA, SIMA, weight alignment, EMA gradients, rank r, number of blocks N_B), and a careful cost analysis (Sec. A.6, Tab. 10) shows the method adds only ~5% memory and ~10% FLOPs over SFT, which is a practical advantage over distillation-based and dual-adapter baselines.

The fast-adaptation experiments (Fig. 5, Fig. 11) demonstrate a useful practical benefit beyond final accuracy, and the CKA analysis (Sec. A.7) provides empirical support for the block-wise aggregation design.
weaknesses: Model heterogeneity is weaker than the framing suggests: all heterogeneous clients are LLaVA variants sharing the identical CLIP ViT-L/336px vision encoder and differing only in LLM backbone size (and even then, mostly within the same family). Real architectural heterogeneity (different hidden dims across families, different vision encoders, different depths/attention patterns) is only partially tested (three variants in Sec. A.8). The claim of a 'more general heterogeneous setup' is stronger than the evidence.

Some technical components appear heuristic or under-justified. In particular, the B-matrix alignment formula in Eq. 21 / Algorithm 4 appears inconsistent (as written, ((Π_i)^{-1})^T (Π_i)^T collapses to identity, and the inverse of a CCA projection matrix is not guaranteed to exist or be numerically stable). The main text (Sec. 4.2.2) and Algorithm 4 do not agree, which raises correctness concerns.

The theoretical results are close to trivial: Theorem 1 (orthogonal outer products span an r²-dimensional space) and Theorem 2 (freezing A and B makes aggregation error zero, essentially by definition) provide little insight into when PQ-LoRA preserves knowledge transfer quality across heterogeneous models, which is the actual question of interest.

Personalization ('Self') gains over SFT are modest (typically 1–4% average, with some clients showing no gain or small losses, e.g., Tab. 3 clients 2–3, Tab. 19). The strongest gains are on 'Others' (generalization), and the paper's framing relies on arguing that generalization matters for future personalization; a stronger direct demonstration of end-to-end value would help.

The scale remains limited relative to the real-world claims: 10 clients, 20 communication rounds, memory-infinite replay (all past data stored and resampled), and task assignment fixed a priori. This weakens the 'bridging simulated and real-world FL' narrative; the authors acknowledge the client-count limitation but the memory-infinite assumption also contradicts the streaming-data motivation.

The method is a fairly complex combination of components (EMA-decayed gradients of a small frozen model, MSE alignment with orthogonality regularization, SVD post-processing, CCA alignment, softmax-temperature weighting, learnable per-layer gating). While each is ablated, the overall design risks brittleness, and sensitivity to key hyperparameters (α, τ, m) is not fully characterized.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely under-explored and practical problem: personalized federated learning under *both* data and model (cross-family, cross-size) heterogeneity, whereas prior PFL/LLM-FL work typically addresses only one axis or uses simplified setups (e.g., LoRA-rank variation only).

The proposed FedMosaic combines two reasonable and well-motivated components: RELA (task-relevance-weighted aggregation via EMA-decayed, sanitized last-layer gradients from a small frozen model) and PQ-LoRA (dimension-invariant shareable modules with block-wise aggregation and weight alignment via L2/CCA).

The evaluation is unusually thorough: multiple benchmarks (DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-Scope, Fed-Aya, Fed-LLM-Large), static/dynamic distribution-shift setups, homogeneous vs. heterogeneous and cross-family configurations, a large-scale 52-client experiment, fast-adaptation evaluation on unseen tasks, component ablations (Tables 7, 30, 32), and hyperparameter sweeps (rounds/local steps, rank r, N_B, temperature, EMA ratio, noise scale, public data size/domain).

Careful cost accounting: computational, memory, and communication overheads are measured against SFT and baselines (Tables 15, Fig. 7, Sec. A.8-A.9), showing ~10% overhead, which strengthens the practicality claim.

The proposed DRAKE benchmark (40 multi-modal tasks from 19 datasets, multi-image inputs, temporal distribution shifts, and unseen-task generalization splits) fills a real gap in multi-modal FL evaluation, and per-client task configurations and dataset construction are documented in detail.

Numerous experimental details (client model allocation, memory-only training protocol, fair compute-matched local steps, seeds/stds) support reproducibility, and the authors commit to releasing code and the benchmark.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: RELA is essentially similarity-weighted federated aggregation (related ideas exist in pFedSim, pFedHR, FEDLAW, Flashback; the authors acknowledge and compare, but the deltas—frozen-model last-layer gradients plus EMA—are engineering refinements rather than a new conceptual advance). Theorem 2 (zero aggregation error when A, B are frozen) is essentially by definition, and Theorem 1 is a straightforward linear-algebra observation.

The PFL-Dynamic protocol relies on a memory-infinite episodic replay setup (all past samples stored and re-sampled); this is a strong and somewhat unrealistic assumption that arguably weakens the claimed realism of the 'challenging, real-world' dynamic setting, and it is unclear how results would transfer to true streaming/memory-constrained FL.

Privacy claims are informal: gradient noise and random subsampling are presented as mitigating gradient-inversion attacks, but no formal privacy guarantee (e.g., DP analysis) is provided, and the privacy-utility trade-off is only qualitatively analyzed (Fig. 18).

The 'Others' (generalization) evaluation on other clients' data has a somewhat ambiguous interpretation—evaluating a personally-tuned model on other clients' tasks is a proxy for generalization whose significance relative to unseen-task adaptation could be better justified; also, per-task/task-family weighting behind the averages is under-specified in the main text.

Some tasks in DRAKE are constructed by LLM/keyword-based splitting of existing datasets (e.g., GQA subsets, VizWiz subsets, Co-Instruct question-type splits), so 'task heterogeneity' partially reflects artificial partitions rather than genuinely distinct client use cases; validation of these splits (human checks) is not described.

Gains over the strongest baselines vary: on HFLB and Fed-Scope, several baselines (e.g., FedIT, TAKFL, FedDAT) are competitive on 'Self', and average improvements in some tables are modest, with gains concentrated on complex tasks; cross-family experiments require PQ-LoRA alignment for the proposed method but it is unclear how baselines are adapted under cross-family setups and whether alignment itself is a major source of the gain.

Presentation issues: multiple typos/grammar errors ('relevence', 'clinets', 'Homonegeous', 'deacying', 'ins hetero'), an outlier FedDPA number in Table 2 (70.06 vs. ~79 for peers, likely a typo), and heavy reliance on the appendix for core details (public data D_p, pseudocode, algorithms), which slightly hurts readability.

strengths: The paper tackles a realistic and under-explored problem: jointly handling data heterogeneity (distinct multi-modal tasks, temporal distribution shifts) and model heterogeneity (different LLM families/sizes) in personalized federated learning, moving beyond non-i.i.d. splits of a single dataset.

The proposed DRAKE benchmark is substantial: 40 tasks from 19 multi-modal datasets, multi-image inputs, unseen-task splits for generalization evaluation, and a useful comparison table against prior FL benchmarks (Tab. 1).

The evaluation is unusually broad: multiple benchmarks (DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-Scope, Fed-Aya, Fed-LLM-Large with 52 clients), multiple heterogeneous configurations (within-family, cross-family, 1B/3B/8B), strong baseline coverage (8 SOTA PFL methods), extensive ablations (A.17–A.22), and cost analyses for computation, memory, and communication.

PQ-LoRA's dimension-invariant P (r×r) and Q (r) modules are a simple and communication-efficient mechanism for sharing adapters across architectures with different hidden dimensions and depths, supported by ablations on block count and weight alignment.
Per-client analyses (Tab. 5, 21–25) honestly show where gains over SFT are small or negative, and the paper correctly identifies SFT as a strong personalization baseline.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty of RELA: similarity-weighted aggregation via cosine similarity of client gradients is a well-studied idea (acknowledged in A.22 against pFedSim, pFedHR, etc.). The EMA decay and sanitized-gradient variants are incremental refinements rather than a new mechanism.

The theoretical contributions are weak. Theorem 2 (zero aggregation error when A and B are frozen) is essentially vacuous — freezing parameters trivially makes the averaged-product equal the product-of-averages — and the 'aggregation error' framing sidesteps the real question of whether freezing A, B (trained only via alignment on public data) limits adaptation capacity, which is empirically visible in the N_B trade-off (Tab. 29).

The privacy claims are informal and possibly overstated: adding Gaussian noise with µ = 1e-4 and random subsampling does not constitute a formal DP guarantee, and gradient-inversion resistance is asserted by citation rather than demonstrated (e.g., no attack experiments).

Potential circularity between benchmark and method: the strongest gains are reported on the self-proposed DRAKE benchmark, whose task splits are constructed using LLM (GPT-4) categorization, introducing possible labeling noise and a risk that the benchmark favors the proposed approach; HFLB results show much smaller margins.

The RELA similarity signal is fragile: task relevance is computed from last-layer gradients of a separate small frozen model (Ws), which measures data similarity, not the knowledge actually being exchanged between heterogeneous adapter updates; the 'decayed frozen gradients' ablation (Tab. 30) shows only ~1-point differences, within a plausible noise band given ±0.5–1.2 std across seeds.

The method requires alignment on public data Dp before federated training, partially undermining the stated privacy/realism narrative, and the claimed robustness to domain mismatch (Tab. 27) uses only a handful of Dp choices.

Evaluation is confined to LLaVA-style MLLMs and Llama-3 text models; claims of generality across architectures (e.g., non-transformer backbones) are deferred to future work, and all heterogeneous settings involve models sharing a common lineage (Llama/Qwen LLaVA variants) rather than truly diverse architectures.

Writing quality is below bar for a top-tier venue: repeated typos ('clinets', 'relevantce', 'ins', 'vws'), inconsistent notation between the paper and Algorithm 1 (e.g., g_t vs g[i], EMA over per-round averaged sanitized gradients differs from Eq. 2's per-batch recursion), and a missing FedDAT row-value anomaly (70.06 vs 79.87 pattern in Tab. 2 FedDPA) that suggests insufficient proofreading.
Reproducibility is uncertain: most baselines must be re-implemented on the new benchmark, and code is only promised ('will definitely release') rather than provided.

strengths: The paper addresses a realistic and important gap in personalized federated learning: jointly handling both data heterogeneity (diverse tasks, temporal distribution shifts) and model heterogeneity (different architectures/families/scales), where prior work tackles at most one under simplified assumptions.

The proposed FedMosaic is technically well-motivated and composed of two complementary components: RELA (relevance-guided aggregation using decayed, sanitized last-layer gradients from a small frozen model to weight aggregation by task relatedness) and PQ-LoRA (dimension-invariant modules P, Q that enable cross-architecture sharing, with block-wise aggregation and weight alignment via L2/CCA). The design choices are carefully reasoned.

The DRAKE benchmark is a substantial contribution in its own right: 40 heterogeneous multi-modal tasks from 19 datasets with temporal distribution shifts and unseen-task evaluation, filling a clear gap relative to existing FL benchmarks (which are mostly non-i.i.d. splits of a single dataset or single-task).

The evaluation is unusually thorough: heterogeneous, cross-family, homogeneous, and text-only setups; scale-up to 52 clients; ablations of both components; extensive hyperparameter analyses (rank, NB, temperature, EMA ratio, sampling ratio, noise scale, public data size/domain); fast-adaptation evaluation on unseen tasks; and cost analyses showing modest computational/memory overhead (~10% over SFT) and even reduced communication cost vs. FedAvg.

Theoretical support is provided: Theorem 1 (orthogonality of A, B maximizes span of PQ-LoRA updates, proven in A.2) and Theorem 2 (freezing A, B achieves zero aggregation error), with honest discussion of assumptions.
The paper is candid about when gains are large vs. small (per-client analysis in Tab. 5 shows SFT suffices for simple single-image tasks), which increases credibility.
Comprehensive ablations of RELA (Tab. 30) and alignment (Tab. 32) validate each design decision, and the empirical CKA analysis (Fig. 11) supports the block-wise relative-depth alignment assumption.
weaknesses: Privacy claims are informal: gradient sanitization (noise + subsampling) is argued to mitigate gradient inversion, but no formal guarantee (e.g., differential privacy budget) is given; the trade-off between the privacy mechanisms and RELA's reliance on gradient similarity deserves more rigorous treatment.

The DRAKE benchmark construction relies on LLM-based (GPT-4) categorization of samples into tasks; potential noise in task labels and its effect on conclusions are not analyzed, and benchmark quality depends heavily on this step.

Model diversity, while broader than prior work, is still confined to LLaVA-1.5-based variants with CLIP vision encoders and Llama/Qwen LLM backbones; generalization to truly dissimilar architectures (e.g., different vision encoders, convolutional models) is deferred to future work.

The block-wise aggregation relies on an approximately linear relative-depth alignment assumption validated only for Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 families; it is unclear how well this extends to more architecturally divergent models.

The 'Others' generalization metric aggregates performance on other clients' tasks, which may conflate effects of model capacity differences (1B vs. 3B) with genuine knowledge transfer; a more fine-grained analysis of cross-client transfer structure would strengthen the claims.

Weight alignment requires access to public data Dp (LLaVA-Instruct-158K), which is an extra assumption not available in all federated settings; although Tab. 27 shows robustness to Dp choice, the necessity of Dp is a limitation.

Some improvements over the strongest baselines (FedIT, FedDPA) on 'Self' metrics are moderate in places, and part of the gain narrative rests on complex-task clients; the paper handles this reasonably but the headline numbers may overstate typical gains.
